record.context_brief: AGN seeds in enhanced ALP-density regions
record.original_question: In ALP regions whose density is enhanced enough to allow galaxy formation at redshifts z > 10, as suggested as an explanation of JWST early-galaxy observations, does a black hole form in the central part of each enhanced-density region, or can the enhanced ALP density itself act as the seed of an active galactic nucleus in early galaxies?

evidence.quote: the ALP density in the surrounding regions is much higher than the average in the Universe and the galaxy formation in these regions can take place much earlier, than in the rest of the Universe and can happen at the redshifts z > 10, as indicated by the data of JWST [37].

In particular, the question is of special interest whether black hole formation is possible in their central part, or the enhanced ALP density itself plays the role of AGN seeds in the early galaxies.

artifact.category_tag: ALP dark matter and AGN seed formation
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a cosmological model in which the dark matter consists, at least in part, of axion-like particles (ALPs): light pseudo-scalar bosons coupled gravitationally to ordinary matter. Suppose that, due to non-linear field dynamics or to topological/inhomogeneous initial conditions, the ALP energy density is spatially inhomogeneous, so that there exist localized regions in which the ALP density is substantially larger than the cosmological mean. Assume the enhancement is sufficient that gravitational collapse and galaxy formation inside such an over-dense region can occur at redshifts z > 10, consistent with the existence of unexpectedly luminous, massive early galaxies observed at such redshifts.

Within this setup, address the following question. In the central part of each ALP over-dense region in which an early galaxy forms, determine whether:

(a) ordinary gravitational collapse of baryonic matter (and possibly of the ALP component itself) inevitably produces a central black hole that can act as the seed of an active galactic nucleus (AGN), and characterize the expected mass spectrum and formation redshift of such seeds; or

(b) the enhanced ALP density configuration itself — for example a soliton, boson star, or other coherent ALP condensate at the center of the over-dense region — can play the dynamical role of an AGN seed, mimicking the gravitational and (eventually) accretion-driven phenomenology of a central massive black hole without requiring an actual horizon.

Provide quantitative criteria (in terms of the ALP mass m_a, self-coupling, local density contrast, and host halo mass) distinguishing regime (a) from regime (b), and determine which regime is realized in physically motivated ALP models compatible with the observed early-galaxy population.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether AGN seeds in JWST-observed high-redshift galaxies originate from gravitational collapse to black holes or from coherent ALP/ultralight-dark-matter condensates (solitons, boson stars) acting as effective seeds is an active area of investigation. No consensus or definitive resolution has been established; the question appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Open questions of BSM Cosmology
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses ALP over-dense regions and the open question of whether black holes form in their centers or whether enhanced ALP density itself seeds AGN.
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly posed as open.
